title: Who, what, where, when
goal: Master the ten Irish question words and the letter changes they bring.
bekal: use *cé, cad, cá, cathain, conas, cén fáth, cé mhéad* correctly
know which words bring séimhiú and which bring urú

notes: **Irish has no helper words like "do" standing on their own.** You make a question by swapping the first word of the sentence. *Tá sé anseo* ("he is here") becomes *An bhfuil sé anseo?* ("is he here?") or *Cá bhfuil sé?* ("where is he?"). The rest of the sentence doesn't move at all — much simpler than English, which has to flip the word order and add *do* as well.

**Cén is cé + an, and it is always followed by a noun.** *Cén t-am?* (what time), *Cén aois?* (what age), *Cén sórt?* (what kind), *Cén fáth?* (what reason, i.e. why), *Cén dath?* (what color). Because *cén* already contains the article *an*, don't add another *an*: *Cén t-am é?*, not *Cén an t-am é?*

**Cé hé, cé hí — the h slips in again.** To ask who someone is, use *Cé hé sin?* (a man), *Cé hí sin?* (a woman), *Cé hiad sin?* (plural). The *h* appears because the next word starts with a vowel — the same pattern as *go hiontach*, *a hocht*, and *ní hea* from earlier units.

**Cé mhéad — with séimhiú, and a singular noun.** *Cé mhéad euro?*, *Cé mhéad duine?*, *Cé mhéad leabhar?* The word *méad* is softened because it comes after *cé*, and the noun is never made plural. To ask a price, the most common form is *Cé mhéad atá air?* — literally "how much is on it?", using the same *ar* pattern as *Tá ocras orm*.

blocks.text: *Cad* and *céard* mean the same and are equally correct; *cad* is more common in the south, *céard* in Connacht. To ask about a thing you are pointing at, both usually go with *é*: *Cad é sin?* or *Céard é sin?* — "what's that?"

blocks.title: Cén t-am, cén chaoi — why the letters change
items: *Cén* contains the article *an*, so the noun after it behaves exactly as after an ordinary *an* (Unit 4). **Masculine** words starting with a vowel get *t-*: *cén t-am*, *cén t-ainm*.
**Feminine** words get séimhiú: *cén chaoi* (from *caoi*), *cén cheist* (from *ceist*), *cén bhliain* (from *bliain*).
So there's no new rule to learn — just remember that *cén* = *cé* + *an*, and everything you already know about *an* applies as is.

blocks.text: Now the pattern can be gathered together. For the rest of this book, these are the words that most often change a first letter.

blocks.title: If the verb starts with a vowel
items: A vowel can't be softened or eclipsed, so usually nothing happens: *ní ólaim*, *an ólann tú?*
The exceptions are *cá*, *go*, and *nach*, which put **n-** before a vowel: *cá n-itheann tú?*, *go n-ólann sé*, *nach n-itheann tú?*
The letters *l, n, r* never change either — no séimhiú and no urú for these three. *Ní labhraím*, *an labhraíonn tú?*
